facts.text: kunanyi/Mount Wellington rises above Hobart, Tasmania, and draws more than 400,000 visitors a year, most of whom drive up a winding road to the summit.
Car access to the summit is often closed in the colder months because of snow and ice on the only road.
A cable car to the summit was first proposed in 1905, before the first road to the top had been built; other plans followed in 1931 and 2004.
The latest plan, by the Mount Wellington Cableway Company, was a $54 million cable car running more than two kilometres from the base of the mountain to the summit.
The plan included three towers, two cable cars, a base station in South Hobart, and a new summit centre with a restaurant and cafe, up to 11.4 metres tall.
The plan drew a record 16,537 public submissions, and nearly 10,000 people watched the council meeting about it online.
In July 2021 Hobart City Council voted 9 to 3 to reject the plan, after an independent planning report listed 21 grounds for refusal.
The planners found the cable car would reduce the tourism, recreation, cultural and landscape values of the mountain; concerns included safety, noise, nearby homes, the environment and views.
The cableway would have passed in front of the Organ Pipes, the mountain’s best-known cliffs.
One councillor said the summit centre would damage an alpine plant community that had developed over centuries.

In November 2022 Tasmania’s planning tribunal rejected the company’s appeal, finding the plan failed standards on noise, visual impact, geological heritage and biodiversity; the company did not appeal further.
It was the eighth cable car proposal for the mountain in a century, but the first to be formally lodged and tested under planning rules.
Opponents said the real task was to stop the mountain from being loved to death and to invest in facilities that protect its natural values.
Supporters of the company described the existing summit facilities and road as poor and in need of improvement.
In May 2024 the Tasmanian government announced a 12-month review of how the mountain and the surrounding Wellington Park are managed.
Of more than 9,000 public submissions to the review, 30 per cent said they supported a cable car and 28 per cent said they opposed one.
Draft recommendations from the review included a cable car; officials pointed to a need for all-weather access and other ways of reaching the summit.
The park’s management trust said the park exists partly to provide recreation and tourism, but not to actively increase the number of visitors.
About 450,000 people visited Wellington Park in 2024; without changes, visitor numbers are forecast to double over the next 25 years to about 910,000.
Around 500,000 vehicles go up the mountain each year, according to an ABC calculation.
A 2026 consultancy report suggested charging private cars and shuttle buses, raising about $8.6 million a year and cutting visitor numbers by about 29 per cent, or 183,000 people.
The report described the expected fall in visitors as a deliberate and positive result that would reduce crowding and pressure on nature; walkers would not be charged.
The Organ Pipes are columns of dolerite up to 120 metres high, formed during the Jurassic period when molten rock cooled underground.
As of June 2026, the government’s final action plan for the mountain had not been published.
